The Implicit Bias of Adam and Muon on Smooth Homogeneous Neural Networks

Eitan Gronich   Gal Vardi Weizmann Institute of Science {eitan.gronich, gal.vardi}@weizmann.ac.il
Abstract

We study the implicit bias of momentum-based optimizers on homogeneous models. We first extend existing results on the implicit bias of steepest descent in homogeneous models to normalized steepest descent with an optional learning rate schedule. We then show that for smooth homogeneous models, momentum steepest descent algorithms like Muon (spectral norm), MomentumGD (ℓ2\ell_{2} norm), and Signum (ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm) are approximate steepest descent trajectories under a decaying learning rate schedule, proving that these algorithms too have a bias towards KKT points of the corresponding margin maximization problem. We extend the analysis to Adam (without the stability constant), which maximizes the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} margin, and to Muon-Signum and Muon-Adam, which maximize a hybrid norm. Our experiments corroborate the theory and show that the identity of the margin maximized depends on the choice of optimizer. Overall, our results extend earlier lines of work on steepest descent in homogeneous models and momentum-based optimizers in linear models.

1 Introduction

Deep neural networks show remarkable generalization performance despite often being overparameterized, and even when trained with no explicit regularization. A well-established line of work attempts to explain this phenomenon with the notion of the implicit bias (tendency) of gradient-based optimization algorithms to converge to well-generalizing solutions. This bias is often realized in the form of maximizing a certain margin for the training points (cf. Vardi (2023)).

While earlier works studied mostly gradient descent and showed its implicit bias towards maximizing the ℓ2\ell_{2} margin in increasingly complex models, recent years have witnessed an interest in the study of the implicit bias of other optimizers, such as Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015), AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), and recently Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), hand-in-hand with their rising popularity. Indeed, as these algorithms are used near-universally for training large language models (LLMs) and vision transformers, there is a growing imperative to understand their inner workings.

In this work, we study smooth homogeneous models and show a margin-maximization bias of Adam and Muon. Previous work analyzed the implicit bias of Adam and Muon on linear predictors (Zhang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025), and we extend these results to the substantially broader class of smooth homogeneous models. Moreover, our analysis of Muon is a special case of a more general framework that we develop, which is applicable to all momentum-based optimizers built on top of steepest descent algorithms. All of our results hold for a family of exponentially tailed losses that includes the logistic and exponential losses.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We show that any limit point of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} in a normalized steepest descent trajectory with a learning rate schedule η⁡(t)\eta(t) is a KKT point of the ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert-max-margin problem, as long as ∫0∞η⁡(t)​𝑑t=∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta(t)dt=\infty. This result holds for any locally Lipschitz, C1C^{1}-stratifiable homogeneous model, including ReLU networks. It extends a result by Tsilivis et al. (2025) that considered (unnormalized) steepest descent with a constant learning rate.

  2. 2.

    We show that when 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} converges, it converges to the direction of a KKT point of the ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert-max-margin problem even for trajectories which approximate steepest descent. This allows us to focus on momentum-based optimizers on smooth homogeneous models and show:

    1. (a)

      Muon has an implicit bias towards margin maximization with respect to a norm defined using spectral norms of the weight matrices, under a decaying learning rate regime. In fact, the bias towards margin maximization holds for any normalized Momentum Steepest Descent (MSD) algorithm, for the appropriate norm. We show this includes composite MSD algorithms such as Muon-Signum. In addition, we prove an implicit bias of Muon-Adam.

    2. (b)

      Adam (without the stability constant) has an implicit bias towards ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} margin maximization under a decaying learning rate regime.

Related Work

Soudry et al. (2018) first showed that gradient descent in linear models maximizes the ℓ2\ell_{2} margin. This result was followed by several works on margin maximization in linear fully-connected, convolutional and diagonal networks (e.g., Ji and Telgarsky (2018); Gunasekar et al. (2018a); Yun et al. (2020); Moroshko et al. (2020)). Going beyond linear networks, Chizat and Bach (2020) studied the implicit bias in infinitely-wide two-layer smooth homogeneous networks, and proved margin maximization w.r.t. a certain function norm, known as the variation norm. Lyu and Li (2019) studied homogeneous models under gradient descent, demonstrating that any limit point of the direction of the vector of parameters 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is the direction of a KKT point of the max-margin problem. In a complementary result, Ji and Telgarsky (2020) showed that directional convergence of the parameters is indeed guaranteed when optimizing homogeneous models definable in an o-minimal structure with gradient descent. The implicit bias of gradient descent in certain non-homogeneous neural networks was studied in Nacson et al. (2019a); Kunin et al. (2022); Cai et al. (2025). For a more comprehensive survey on the implicit bias of gradient descent, see Vardi (2023).

A general treatment of the implicit bias of the family of steepest descent algorithms was given for linear models by Gunasekar et al. (2018b), who proved maximization of the appropriate norm-dependent margin. Tsilivis et al. (2025) generalized that result and the result by Lyu and Li (2019) and proved for homogeneous models under steepest descent that any limit point of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is a KKT point of the max-margin problem.

Adam in the context of homogeneous models was studied by Wang et al. (2021), who showed a bias towards ℓ2\ell_{2}-margin maximization. Notably, this work studied Adam without momentum in the numerator and with a stability constant ε\varepsilon which asymptotically dominates the denominator, driving behavior to be similar to gradient descent. Follow-up works have argued that the analysis of the implicit bias with the stability constant is less faithful to the characteristics of Adam in practice, as the stability constant is typically negligible throughout the trajectory. Such works on Adam without the stability constant have so far focused on linear models and include Zhang et al. (2024) and Fan et al. (2025), in the binary and multiclass settings respectively, who showed ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} margin maximization, and Baek et al. (2025) who showed that the implicit bias of Adam under a deterministic batching routine can deviate from the full-batch case. We generalize the result by Zhang et al. (2024) to smooth homogeneous models. AdamW, contrasting with other algorithms by its utilization of explicit weight decay, was studied for smooth models and losses by Xie and Li (2024), who showed that limit points of the trajectory are KKT points of the loss under the constraint that the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm of the parameters is bounded.

Fan et al. (2025) studied normalized steepest descent and its momentum counterparts on linear models in the multiclass setting, including spectral descent and Muon respectively, and showed maximization of the appropriate margins. We generalize their result, albeit in the binary classification setting.

2 Preliminaries

Throughout this work, we consider a fixed binary classification dataset {(𝐱i,yi)}i=1m⊆ℝd×{±1}\{\left(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i}\right)\}_{i=1}^{m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\{\pm 1\}, a parameterized model f⁡(𝐱,𝜽)f(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}) for parameters 𝜽∈ℝp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, and a log-concave, exponentially tailed loss of the form:

where φ\varphi is twice continuously differentiable, strictly monotone increasing and convex, with bounded first and second derivatives (see Appendix C.1), notably allowing for the exponential (ℓ⁡(u)=e−u\ell(u)=e^{-u}) and logistic (ℓ⁡(u)=log⁡(1+e−u)\ell(u)=\log(1+e^{-u})) losses. For a vector 𝐯∈ℝn\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} we denote by 𝐯⁡[j]\mathbf{v}[j] the jj’th coordinate of 𝐯\mathbf{v}. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we denote [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}. 2.2 Optimizers

The optimization algorithms we study are derivatives of the steepest descent family, a generalization of gradient descent defined with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert (and its dual norm ‖⋅‖⋆{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\star}). We study the infinitesimal step size (flow) limit of the optimization trajectories. We define steepest descent and its normalized variant in the general case of a subdifferentiable model ff, allowing for a learning rate schedule η⁡(t)>0\eta(t)>0, as follows:

Steepest Descent:

d​𝜽td​t∈{η⁡(t)⋅arg⁡min‖𝐮‖=‖𝐠t‖⋆​⟨𝐮,𝐠t⟩∣𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)},\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\in\left\{\eta(t)\cdot\arg\min_{\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert={\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rangle\mid\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\}~, (2)

Normalized Steepest Descent:

d​𝜽td​t∈{η⁡(t)⋅arg⁡min‖𝐮‖=1​⟨𝐮,𝐠t⟩∣𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)},\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\in\left\{\eta(t)\cdot\arg\min_{\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert=1}\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rangle\mid\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\}~, (3)

for almost every t≥0t\geq 0, where ∂ℒ\partial\mathcal{L} is the Clarke subdifferential of ℒ\mathcal{L} (see Appendix A), which reduces to ∇ℒ\nabla\mathcal{L} wherever ff is differentiable. Notably, gradient descent and coordinate descent are recovered with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖2,‖⋅‖1\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{1} respectively from Equation 2, and sign gradient descent is recovered with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖∞\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\infty} from Equation 3.

Introducing momentum-based optimizers, we consider a choice of subgradients 𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) along the trajectory, and denote the momentum estimate by the following ODE with the given explicit solution:

d​𝐦td​t=c1​(𝐠t−𝐦t),𝐦0=𝟎(Explicitly:𝐦t=∫0tc1e−c1​(t−s)𝐠sds).\begin{gathered}\frac{d\mathbf{m}_{t}}{dt}=c_{1}(\mathbf{g}_{t}-\mathbf{m}_{t}),\quad\mathbf{m}_{0}=\mathbf{0}\\ \left(\text{Explicitly:}\quad\mathbf{m}_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}c_{1}e^{-c_{1}(t-s)}\mathbf{g}_{s}ds\right)~.\end{gathered} (4)

For the full derivation of the above continuous analogue of momentum, see Appendix B. Here, c1>0c_{1}>0 is the momentum smoothing parameter, and 1c1\frac{1}{c_{1}} is the characteristic time frame in which past gradients are accumulated (c1c_{1} is analogous to −log⁡(β1)-\log(\beta_{1}) for a discrete momentum parameter β1∈(0,1)\beta_{1}\in(0,1), and is roughly 1−β11-\beta_{1} when β1\beta_{1} is close to 1). We now define momentum steepest descent and its normalized counterpart:

Momentum Steepest Descent:

d​𝜽td​t∈{η⁡(t)⋅arg⁡min‖𝐮‖=‖𝐦t‖⋆​⟨𝐮,𝐦t⟩},\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\in\left\{\eta(t)\cdot\arg\min_{\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert={\left\lVert\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\rangle\right\}~, (5)

Normalized Momentum Steepest Descent:

d​𝜽td​t∈{η⁡(t)⋅arg⁡min‖𝐮‖=1​⟨𝐮,𝐦t⟩}.\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\in\left\{\eta(t)\cdot\arg\min_{\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert=1}\left\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\rangle\right\}~. (6)

Classical gradient descent with momentum, for example, is obtained from Equation (5) with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖2\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}. Muon, the recently proposed weight-matrix optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024), applies Newton-Schulz orthogonalization iterations on a momentum estimate of the matrix. In our work (as in Fan et al. (2025)), Muon refers to the exact orthogonalization setting rather than the Netwon-Schulz approximation (i.e., U​Σ​VT↦U​VTU\Sigma V^{T}\mapsto UV^{T} where U​Σ​VTU\Sigma V^{T} is the SVD of the weight matrix WW). Muon with exact orthogonalization is recovered from Equation 6 with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖sp\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert={\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{sp}} for a single-layer network. When running Muon simultaneously on each weight matrix of a multi-layer network, the resulting trajectory follows Equation 6 with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖msp\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert={\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{msp}} (see notations in Subsection 2.1). Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) noted that Shampoo with accumulation disabled is, too, spectral descent, although accumulation in Shampoo is not identical to momentum. Another algorithm adhering exactly to Equation (6) is Signum (Bernstein et al., 2018), i.e. momentum sign gradient descent (‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖∞\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\infty}).

The final optimizer we discuss is Adam, for which we define similarly to the above

d​𝐯td​t=c2​(𝐠t2−𝐯t),𝐯0=𝟎(Explicitly:𝐯t=∫0tc2e−c2​(t−s)𝐠s2ds),\begin{gathered}\frac{d\mathbf{v}_{t}}{dt}=c_{2}(\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}-\mathbf{v}_{t}),\quad\mathbf{v}_{0}=\mathbf{0}\\ \left(\text{Explicitly:}\quad\mathbf{v}_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}c_{2}e^{-c_{2}(t-s)}\mathbf{g}_{s}^{2}ds\right)~,\end{gathered} (7)

where the square is taken element-wise. Following Zhang et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2025); Baek et al. (2025); Xie and Li (2024), we consider Adam without the stability constant, as this setting more accurately reflects the behavior of Adam in practice, where the stability constant is typically negligible throughout the trajectory. Therefore we define Adam as the following:

Adam:d​𝜽td​t=−η(t)⋅𝐦^t𝐯^t,\text{{Adam:}}\quad\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}=-\eta(t)\cdot\frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}}}~, (8)

where 𝐦^t=(1−e−c1​t)−1​𝐦t\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}=(1-e^{-c_{1}t})^{-1}\mathbf{m}_{t} and 𝐯^t=(1−e−c2​t)−1​𝐯t\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}=(1-e^{-c_{2}t})^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{t} are bias-corrected terms, and division and square root are taken element-wise. Adam in the discrete case (Kingma and Ba (2015)) is defined using parameters β1,β2∈[0,1)\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in[0,1), where β1≤β2\beta_{1}\leq\beta_{2} (see definition for the discrete case in Appendix B).11 1 Pytorch (Paszke et al., 2019) defaults are β1=0.9,β2=0.999\beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999. Due to the inverse relation between βi\beta_{i} and cic_{i}, this is analogous to c1≥c2c_{1}\geq c_{2}, which is the setting we focus on.

2.3 Assumptions

We now introduce the assumptions made in this work. Note that some assumptions overlap, and not all assumptions are used in all sections of the work.

Model Assumptions.

Our main contributions include the following assumptions on ff:

  1. (M1)

    ff is smooth in 𝜽\bm{\theta}, i.e. ∀𝐱∈ℝd:f⁡(𝐱,⋅)∈C1​(ℝp)\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:f(\mathbf{x};\cdot)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{p}).

  2. (M2)

    ff is LL-homogeneous for some L≥1L\geq 1, i.e. ∀𝐱∈ℝd,𝜽∈ℝp,α>0:f⁡(𝐱,α​𝜽)=αL​f​(𝐱,𝜽)\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},\alpha>0:f(\mathbf{x};\alpha\bm{\theta})=\alpha^{L}f(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}).

This includes (deep) linear networks, for which implicit bias has been extensively studied (e.g., Ji and Telgarsky (2018); Gunasekar et al. (2018a); Yun et al. (2020); Moroshko et al. (2020)), but notably also models with smooth non-linear activations such as assumed in Chizat and Bach (2020). One example for an activation function that induces non-linear smooth homogeneous networks is ReLUq​(z):=max⁡{0,z}q\text{ReLU}^{q}(z):=\max\{0,z\}^{q}, for any constant q>1q>1 (networks with this activation function have been studied in, e.g., Cao et al. (2022); Min and Vidal (2024); Min and Vidal (2025); Chizat and Bach (2020)). Another example for a smooth homogeneous activation is the quadratic activation z↦z2z\mapsto z^{2}, which has been studied in many prior works (e.g., Soltanolkotabi et al. (2018); Du and Lee (2018); Gamarnik et al. (2019); Sarao Mannelli et al. (2020); Mohamadi et al. (2024); Martin et al. (2024); Arous et al. (2025); Martin et al. (2026)).

The results for normalized steepest descent have weaker model assumptions:

  1. (M1-Weak)

    ff is locally Lipschitz and Whitney C1C^{1}-stratifiable (thereby admitting a chain rule), see Appendix A.

  2. (M2-Weak)

    ff is LL-homogeneous for some L>0L>0.

In fact, all of our results allow Assumption (M1) to be weakened to (M1-Weak), under a stabilization condition on the trajectory – see Section 4. Notably, networks with ReLU activations satisfy (M1-Weak) but not (M1).

Learning Rate Assumptions.

We detail the different sets of assumptions on the learning rate schedule η⁡(t)\eta(t), according to the setting (normalized steepest descent, momentum steepest descent and Adam).

  1. (LR-NSD)

    η⁡(t)\eta(t) satisfies ∫0∞η⁡(t)​𝑑t=∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta(t)dt=\infty.

  2. (LR-MSD)

    η⁡(t)\eta(t) satisfies ∫0∞η⁡(t)​𝑑t=∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta(t)dt=\infty and η⁡(t)≤o⁡(t1L−1)\eta(t)\leq\mathrm{o}\left(t^{\frac{1}{L}-1}\right), where L≥1L\geq 1 is from (M2).

  3. (LR-Adam)

    η⁡(t)\eta(t) satisfies ∫0∞η⁡(t)​𝑑t=∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta(t)dt=\infty and η⁡(t)≤o⁡(t1L−1)\eta(t)\leq\mathrm{o}\left(t^{\frac{1}{L}-1}\right), where L≥1L\geq 1 is from (M2), and is non-increasing.

We note that existing works on Adam and momentum steepest descent in linear models (Zhang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Baek et al., 2025) assumed a non-increasing learning rate ηt\eta_{t} with ∑t=1∞ηt=∞\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta_{t}=\infty and ηt=o⁡(1)\eta_{t}=\mathrm{o}\left(1\right), as well as additional technical assumptions; our Assumption (LR-Adam) in the linear predictor case (L=1L=1) is somewhat weaker than theirs.

Realizability and Trajectory Assumptions.

For normalized steepest descent, we assume as in Lyu and Li (2019); Tsilivis et al. (2025) and others,

  1. (R1)

    There exists t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 with ℒ⁡(𝜽t0)<ℓ⁡(0)\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t_{0}})<\ell(0).

Assumption (R1) is not assumed in the momentum steepest descent and Adam results; instead we assume the following:

  1. (T1)

    Nontrivial trajectory: ∃Nmin>0,t0≥0:∀t≥t0:‖𝜽t‖≥Nmin\exists N_{\text{min}}>0,t_{0}\geq 0:\forall t\geq t_{0}:\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert\geq N_{\text{min}}.

  2. (T2)

    Directional Convergence: 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} converges to some 𝜽¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} with a positive margin γ⁡(𝜽¯)>0\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0.

Assumption (T1) guarantees only that 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} is eventually bounded away from the origin. In particular this assumption holds if eventually ℒ⁡(𝜽t)<m⋅ℓ⁡(0)−δ\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})<m\cdot\ell(0)-\delta for some δ>0\delta>0. This is therefore a very mild assumption. (T1) follows from (R1) when analyzing (normalized) steepest descent, since the loss is proved to decay once ℒ⁡(𝜽t)<ℓ⁡(0)\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})<\ell(0); momentum steepest descent and Adam, however, only asymptotically approximate steepest descent, and such a decay is only proved for them in this work under Assumptions (T1) and (T2).

Regarding (T2), we note that the directional convergence assumption can be found in the implicit bias literature of linear and homogeneous networks (see, for instance, Gunasekar et al. (2018b); Gunasekar et al. (2018a); Chizat and Bach (2020); Nacson et al. (2019b)). The assumption of a strictly positive margin, which also implies realizability, can also be found in Gunasekar et al. (2018a); Nacson et al. (2019b). We remark that Ji and Telgarsky (2020) showed that directional convergence in homogeneous models definable in an o-minimal structure is guaranteed under gradient descent. However, no such result is known for other optimizers, and we found (T2) to be crucial, as opposed to arguing about arbitrary limit points of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} (as in Lyu and Li (2019) and Tsilivis et al. (2025)), due to the inherent history-preserving nature of momentum-based optimizers.

Adam Well-Definability Assumption.

To discuss Adam without the stability constant and guarantee that 𝐯t​[j]>0\mathbf{v}_{t}[j]>0 for all j∈[p]j\in[p], which is required to prevent division by zero, we introduce the following technical assumption regarding the initialization. This assumption appears in similar form also in Zhang et al. (2024) and Fan et al. (2025), while Baek et al. (2025) assume nonzero coordinates of the input in the iterative batching regime, leading to a similar conclusion.

  1. (A1)

    There exist τ>0,ρ>0\tau>0,\rho>0 such that for all j∈[p]j\in[p] and for almost any t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau], we have 𝐠t​[j]2>ρ\mathbf{g}_{t}[j]^{2}>\rho. These τ\tau and ρ\rho may be arbitrarily small.

2.4 Margin Maximization and KKT Conditions

An important notion when discussing implicit bias is that of the (hard) margin, defined for homogeneous models with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert by

γ⁡(𝜽)=mini∈[m]⁡yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽‖𝜽‖).\gamma(\bm{\theta})=\min_{i\in[m]}y_{i}f\left(\mathbf{x}_{i};\frac{\bm{\theta}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert}\right)~. (9)

Under Assumption (T2), γ⁡(𝜽t)\gamma(\bm{\theta}_{t}) converges to γ⁡(𝜽¯)\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}}). We also consider the following soft margin

γ~​(𝜽)=φ−1​(log⁡1ℒ⁡(𝜽))‖𝜽‖L,\widetilde{\gamma}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{\varphi^{-1}\left(\log\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})}\right)}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert^{L}}~, (10)

as a convenient substitute for γ⁡(𝜽)\gamma(\bm{\theta}). The soft margin approximates the hard margin with a 𝒪⁡(log⁡m‖𝜽‖L)\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log m}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert^{L}}\right) error that vanishes whenever ‖𝜽‖→∞\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert\to\infty (as is indeed proved in all of our results). The examination of quantities relating to γ~\widetilde{\gamma} prove important in the analysis.

Our results pertain to the following objective, known as margin maximization, which is not directly optimized by any of the aforementioned algorithms:

min𝜽∈ℝp⁡12​‖𝜽‖2s.t.∀i∈[m]:yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)≥1.\min_{\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\forall i\in[m]:y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})\geq 1~. (11)

Minimizing the norm ‖𝜽‖\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert while preserving feasibility (∀i∈[m]:yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)≥1\forall i\in[m]:y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})\geq 1) is known to be equivalent to maximizing the margin γ⁡(𝜽)\gamma(\bm{\theta}). For general homogeneous models, Problem (11) is non-convex, and the implicit bias of algorithms towards minimizing it is shown in light of the KKT (Karush-Kuhn-Tucker) conditions, which are local stationarity conditions:

Definition 2.1.

A point 𝜽∈ℝp\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} with yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)≥1y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})\geq 1 for all i∈[m]i\in[m] is said to satisfy the KKT conditions of Problem (11) if there exist 𝐤∈∂12​‖𝜽‖2\mathbf{k}\in\partial\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert^{2}, coefficients λ1,…,λm≥0\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{m}\geq 0 and subgradients 𝐡i∈∂f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽)\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}) with:

  1. 1.

    ∑i=1mλi​yi​𝐡i−𝐤=𝟎\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}y_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i}-\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0};

  2. 2.

    ∑i=1mλi​(yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)−1)=0\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}(y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})-1)=0.

3 Results

In this section, we present our main results. We will discuss the proof ideas in Section 5, with all formal proofs deferred to the appendix.

3.1 Normalized Steepest Descent with a LR Schedule

Our first result, assuming only (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak), (R1), (LR-NSD), extends the analysis of Tsilivis et al. (2025) to the setting of normalized steepest descent with a learning rate schedule. We present this result both as inherently valuable (for instance, it implies implicit bias of sign gradient descent) and as providing motivation for the following sections on normalized momentum-based optimizers, which we show approximate normalized steepest descent. It is worth noting that there are no restrictions on the learning rate schedule η⁡(t)\eta(t) except ∫0∞η=∞\int_{0}^{\infty}\eta=\infty.

The following theorem, following Lyu and Li (2019); Tsilivis et al. (2025), shows that once the loss decreases below the interpolation threshold ℓ⁡(0)\ell(0), normalized steepest descent guarantees a monotone increase of the soft margin γ~​(𝜽t)\widetilde{\gamma}(\bm{\theta}_{t}).

Theorem 3.1.

Let 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} be a trajectory of normalized steepest descent with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert (Equation (3)). Under Assumptions (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak), (R1), (LR-NSD), the soft margin γ~​(𝛉t)\widetilde{\gamma}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) is non-decreasing on [t0,∞)[t_{0},\infty).

Next, we prove that any limit point of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is a KKT-point of the appropriate max-margin problem.

Theorem 3.2.

Let 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} be a trajectory of normalized steepest descent with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert (Equation (3)). Under Assumptions (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak), (R1), (LR-NSD), any limit point 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} of 𝛉t‖𝛉t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is the direction of a KKT point of Problem (11) with the same norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert.

3.2 Momentum Steepest Descent, Muon and Muon-Signum

We now consider margin maximization in momentum steepest descent. The following result is based on the general insight that convergence of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} to a KKT point of Problem (11) holds even when the trajectory is only an approximation of steepest descent. We elaborate on the appropriate definition and characteristics of approximate steepest descent in Section 5 and Appendix C.4.

Theorem 3.3.

Let 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} be a trajectory of normalized or unnormalized momentum steepest descent with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert (Equation (6) or (5)). Under Assumptions (M1), (M2), (LR-MSD), (T1), (T2), the limit point 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} of 𝛉t‖𝛉t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is the direction of a KKT point of Problem (11) with the norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert.

Moreover, we show that running multiple normalized (momentum) steepest descent algorithms in parallel on different parts of the parameter vector with respect to different norms is equivalent to a single run of normalized (momentum) steepest descent algorithm relative to the maximal norm among them (see Appendix C.6). As a result we obtain the following corollary on the implicit bias of Muon:

Corollary 3.4.

If 𝛉=(W1,…,WK)\bm{\theta}=(W_{1},...,W_{K}) is a collection of matrices and Muon is run on each matrix simultaneously with the same schedule η⁡(t)\eta(t), then Muon is a case of normalized momentum steepest descent with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖msp\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert={\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{msp}}, and the statement of Theorem 3.3 holds.

When running Muon in practice, often the non-matrix parameters are optimized using Adam (Jordan et al. (2024), Liu et al. (2025)). Adam has been compared to sign gradient descent and Signum (see Orvieto and Gower (2025)) as possible simplifications. Recently, Scion (Pethick et al., 2025) has been proposed, which uses Muon side-by-side with sign gradient descent. This motivates understanding the implicit bias of these “composite” algorithms, to which we contribute the following corollary regarding Muon-Signum, and a theorem for Muon-Adam in Subsection 3.3.

Corollary 3.5.

If 𝛉=(W1,…,WK,𝐮)\bm{\theta}=(W_{1},...,W_{K},\mathbf{u}) is a collection of matrices and additional parameters 𝐮\mathbf{u}, Muon is run on each matrix independently and Signum is run on 𝐮\mathbf{u} with the same schedule η⁡(t)\eta(t), then Muon-Signum is a case of normalized momentum steepest descent with ‖𝛉‖=max⁡{‖(W1,…,WK)‖msp,‖𝐮‖∞}\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert=\max\{{\left\lVert(W_{1},...,W_{K})\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{msp}},\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert_{\infty}\}, and the statement of Theorem 3.3 holds.

3.3 Adam and Muon-Adam

Notably, Adam is not a normalized momentum steepest descent algorithm, as its updates are ratio terms of two momentum estimates of different rates. This makes the case of Adam (and hence also Muon-Adam) especially challenging. Yet, we show that results of the same flavor hold for Adam in the decaying learning rate regime. As discussed after Equation (8), we focus on the parameter regime c1≥c2>0c_{1}\geq c_{2}>0, which is the one more common in practice, as this is equivalent to β1≤β2\beta_{1}\leq\beta_{2}. Here, we will require that η⁡(t)\eta(t) is non-increasing; we stress that η⁡(t)\eta(t) is chosen externally to the algorithm, and in all practical cases of a decaying learning rate, η⁡(t)\eta(t) is chosen to be eventually monotonically decreasing.

Theorem 3.6.

Let 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} be a trajectory of Adam with c1≥c2c_{1}\geq c_{2} (Equation (8)). Under Assumptions (M1), (M2), (LR-Adam), (T1), (T2), (A1), the limit point 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} of 𝛉t‖𝛉t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is the direction of a KKT point of Problem (11) with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖∞\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\infty}.

Next, we consider Muon-Adam. Here, we allow for different momentum parameters and different base learning rates for the Muon and Adam algorithms,22 2 The same generalization can be applied to Muon-Signum, and indeed for the distinct matrices in Muon, in Corollaries 3.5, 3.4. and show the following:

Theorem 3.7.

Assume 𝛉=(W1,…,WK,𝐮)∈ℝp\bm{\theta}=(W_{1},...,W_{K},\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is a parameter vector representing a collection of matrices and additional parameters 𝐮\mathbf{u}. Assume W1,…,WKW_{1},...,W_{K} follow a trajectory of Muon and 𝐮\mathbf{u} follows a trajectory of Adam, with respective learning rates of the form η0M​η​(t),η0A​η​(t)\eta_{0}^{M}\eta(t),\eta_{0}^{A}\eta(t) for η0M,η0A>0\eta_{0}^{M},\eta_{0}^{A}>0 and momentum parameters cMc_{M} for Muon and c1≥c2c_{1}\geq c_{2} for Adam. Assume (M1), (M2), (LR-Adam), (T1), (T2), (A1). Then, the limit point 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} of 𝛉t‖𝛉t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is the direction of a KKT point of Problem (11) with respect to

‖𝜽‖=max⁡{η0Aη0M​‖(W1,…,WK)‖msp,‖𝐮‖∞}.\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert=\max\left\{\frac{\eta_{0}^{A}}{\eta_{0}^{M}}{\left\lVert(W_{1},...,W_{K})\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{msp}},\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert_{\infty}\right\}~.

4 Non-Smooth Models

Our results for momentum steepest descent and Adam are stated under the assumption of smooth models (M1). However, as our proofs (Appendix C.5, C.7) show, this may be weakened to (M1-Weak), if the normalized model subgradients converge. More specifically, denote for all tt subgradients 𝐡⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t)∈∂f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t)\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t})\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t}) for which 𝐠t=−∑i=1mℓ(zit)φ′(zit)yi𝐡(𝐱i;𝜽t)\mathbf{g}_{t}=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell\left(z_{i}^{t}\right)\varphi^{\prime}(z_{i}^{t})y_{i}\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t}). The condition is:

  1. (T3)

    ∀i∈[m]:𝐡⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t)‖𝜽t‖L−1\forall i\in[m]:\frac{\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t})}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert^{L-1}} converges.

Note first that this condition is trivially satisfied for smooth models under (T2): by Theorem B.2(a) in Lyu and Li (2019), it holds that 𝐡⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t)‖𝜽t‖L−1∈∂f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t‖𝜽t‖)\frac{\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t})}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert^{L-1}}\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}). Therefore, for smooth models, i.e., f∈C1f\in C^{1}, convergence of 𝐡⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t)‖𝜽t‖L−1\frac{\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t})}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert^{L-1}} is guaranteed from convergence of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} by continuity of ∇f​(𝐱i,𝜽t)\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t}).

For non-smooth models under (M1-Weak), 𝐡⁡(𝐱i,𝜽t)‖𝜽t‖L−1\frac{\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}_{t})}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert^{L-1}} converges whenever 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} eventually stays in the same C1C^{1} stratum of f⁡(𝐱i,⋅)f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\cdot) (if 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is exactly on a stratum boundary, 𝐡\mathbf{h} can be chosen to conform to any of the bordering strata; the choice of 𝐡\mathbf{h} should be continuous to ensure convergence). In particular, under (T2), this holds whenever the limiting direction 𝜽¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} is an inner point of a stratum. In homogeneous ReLU networks, stratum boundaries are the parameters 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} for which a neuron preactivation is exactly 0. Therefore, when using a consistent choice of ReLU subgradient at 0 (which is always the case in practice), (T3) follows from (T2) for every trajectory in which signs of neuron preactivations eventually stabilize. It is unclear whether this is satisfied in practice or under what conditions; it appears to be violated in our experiments on two-layer ReLU networks with the MNIST dataset, but we leave open the possibility that some settings comply with this condition.

5 Main Proof Ideas

The proofs of Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 follow similar arguments to Tsilivis et al. (2025); hence we skip a detailed description. Of note is the explicit characterization of the rates of ‖𝜽t‖\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert and φ−1​(−log⁡ℒ⁡(𝜽t))\varphi^{-1}(-\log\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})) as ∫0tη\int_{0}^{t}\eta and γ∞⋅(∫0tη)L\gamma_{\infty}\cdot\left(\int_{0}^{t}\eta\right)^{L} respectively (where γ∞\gamma_{\infty} is the asymptotic margin), lacking in the unnormalized analysis of Tsilivis et al. (2025) (see Lemma C.10 for details). Also, as noted by Tsilivis et al. (2025) and Ji and Telgarsky (2020), KKT stationarity of limit points of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} is closely related to alignment of parameters and gradients ⟨𝜽t‖𝜽t‖,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩\left\langle\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle. We extract this insight into a general blueprint that serves us to prove implicit bias results on homogeneous models; namely, Theorem C.8 states that regardless of the optimization algorithm, any limit point 𝜽¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} with γ⁡(𝜽¯)>0\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0 is guaranteed to be a KKT point of Problem (11), if ℒ⁡(𝜽tn)​⟶n→∞​0\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}})\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0 and ⟨𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖,−𝐠tn‖𝐠tn‖⋆⟩​⟶n→∞​1\left\langle\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t_{n}}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}1 on a subsequence tnt_{n} for which 𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖​⟶n→∞​𝜽¯\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\bar{\bm{\theta}}.

5.1 Approximate Steepest Descent

Our main technical contribution is the extension of the KKT stationarity results to approximate steepest descent algorithms and specifically momentum-based algorithms, which we describe here. Steepest descent (normalized or unnormalized) with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert may be described succinctly with the following equation for almost any t≥0t\geq 0:

⟨d​𝜽td​t‖d​𝜽td​t‖,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩=1.\left\langle\frac{\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}}{\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle=1~. (12)

Equation (12) is the linchpin of analyses of steepest descent, as it allows to prove eventual alignment of the (negative) gradients with the parameters themselves. When analyzing momentum-based algorithms, Equation (12) will not be exactly satisfied, but the hope is that a similar relation will hold asymptotically. Hence we define:

Definition 5.1 (Approximate Steepest Descent).

We say that an arc 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} is a trajectory of Approximate Steepest Descent with respect to ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert if there exist ν⁡(t)>0,Rmax>0\nu(t)>0,R_{\text{max}}>0 with:

  1. 1.

    limt→∞N⁡(t):=limt→∞∫0tν=∞\lim_{t\to\infty}N(t):=\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{0}^{t}\nu=\infty;

  2. 2.

    lim supt→∞‖𝜽t‖N⁡(t)≤Rmax\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}{N(t)}\leq R_{\text{max}};

  3. 3.

    ess​liminft→∞⁡r​(t)≥1\essliminf_{t\to\infty}r(t)\geq 1, where

    r⁡(t)​=a.e.​sup𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)⟨1ν⁡(t)​d​𝜽td​t,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩.r(t)\overset{a.e.}{=}\sup_{\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})}\left\langle\frac{1}{\nu(t)}\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle~.

The quantity ν⁡(t)\nu(t) can be chosen in a flexible manner; for momentum steepest descent (and indeed exact steepest descent) ν⁡(t)=‖d​𝜽td​t‖\nu(t)=\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert is chosen, but for Adam we choose ν⁡(t)=η⁡(t)\nu(t)=\eta(t) (the learning rate). Lemma C.15 shows that the properties in Definition 5.1, taken together with a positive lower bound on the margin, suffice to prove that ℒ⁡(𝜽t)​⟶t→∞​0,‖𝜽t‖​⟶t→∞​∞\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0,\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty. Building on this result and on Theorem C.8, in Theorem C.17 we prove that under (T2) and provided that Rmax≤1R_{\text{max}}\leq 1, the limiting direction 𝜽¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} is a KKT point of Problem (11).

5.2 Asymptotic Momentum-Gradient Relations

Our results for momentum steepest descent (MSD) and Adam rely on the analysis of Approximate Steepest Descent. To show that MSD and Adam indeed satisfy Definition 5.1, we analyze the properties of the momentum operator in Appendix B.

In particular, Corollary B.8 offers a key insight, namely that the ratio m⁡(t)g⁡(t)\frac{m(t)}{g(t)} for a real-valued function g⁡(t)g(t) and its momentum estimator m⁡(t)m(t) tends to a well-defined limit whenever d​log⁡gd​t\frac{d\log g}{dt} converges. This is applied in Lemma C.19, which demonstrates, that in our setting of optimization trajectories, when ‖d​𝜽td​t‖≤o⁡(t1L−1)\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert\leq\mathrm{o}\left(t^{\frac{1}{L}-1}\right), it holds that 𝐦t​[j]=𝐠t​[j]​(1±o⁡(1))\mathbf{m}_{t}[j]=\mathbf{g}_{t}[j]\left(1\pm\mathrm{o}\left(1\right)\right) for any coordinate j∈[p]j\in[p] which is momentarily of “significant” magnitude at time tt. This is formalized by observing the set Jε​(t)={j∈[p]∣|𝐠t​[j]|‖𝐠t‖⋆>ε}J_{\varepsilon}(t)=\left\{j\in[p]\mid\frac{\left|\mathbf{g}_{t}[j]\right|}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}>\varepsilon\right\} for an arbitrary ε>0\varepsilon>0. Lemma C.19 also shows that 𝐦t‖𝐦t‖⋆−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆​⟶t→∞​0\frac{\mathbf{m}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{m}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0, which allows proving that MSD is indeed an Approximate Steepest Descent algorithm.

In the analysis of Adam, Lemma C.19 is again vital, as it implies that 𝐦^t​[j]𝐯^t​[j]=sign⁡(𝐠t​[j])​(1±o⁡(1))\frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}[j]}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}}[j]}=\mathrm{sign}\left(\mathbf{g}_{t}[j]\right)(1\pm\mathrm{o}\left(1\right)) whenever 𝐠t​[j]\mathbf{g}_{t}[j] is momentarily significant (as above). The approximation of Adam to sign gradient descent is in fact the essence of showing ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} margin maximization, as sign gradient descent is normalized steepest descent with ‖⋅‖=‖⋅‖∞\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\infty}. However, it is not necessarily true for Adam that ⟨d​𝜽td​t‖d​𝜽td​t‖∞,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖1⟩​⟶t→∞​1\left\langle\frac{\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}}{\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert_{\infty}},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert_{1}}\right\rangle\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}1. Instead, we rely on the flexibility of Definition 5.1, choosing ν⁡(t)=η⁡(t)\nu(t)=\eta(t). We adapt to our setting an important result proved by Zhang et al. (2024) in the discrete case for linear models, which shows that even if momentarily 𝐦^t​[j]𝐯^t​[j]>1\frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{t}[j]}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}[j]}}>1, the opposite holds on average. Namely, we prove in Lemma B.10 that for any j∈[p]j\in[p]

lim supt→∞|𝜽t​[j]|∫0tη=lim supt→∞|∫0tη⁡(s)​𝐦^s​[j]𝐯^s​[j]​𝑑s|∫0tη≤1,\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{\left|\bm{\theta}_{t}[j]\right|}{\int_{0}^{t}\eta}=\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{\left|\int_{0}^{t}\eta(s)\frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{s}[j]}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{s}[j]}}ds\right|}{\int_{0}^{t}\eta}\leq 1~,

allowing us to choose Rmax≤1R_{\text{max}}\leq 1 for Definition 5.1 and finish the proof.

6 Experiments

To validate our findings we train two-layer (one hidden layer) homogeneous networks to classify m=2048m=2048 MNIST digits (LeCun et al., 2002) as even or odd, using the exponential loss. Since our results hold for smooth activations, we use squared ReLU (i.e., z↦max⁡{0,z}2z\mapsto\max\{0,z\}^{2}), and also run ReLU for empirical comparison. We compare the following optimizers: Normalized Gradient Descent (NGD) with and without momentum, Signum, Adam, Muon (treating the output layer as a matrix with a single row) and Muon-Adam. Training proceeds until the loss reaches a small target value (10−810^{-8}). The stability constant for Adam is chosen to be negligible with respect to gradient norm values (ε=10−20\varepsilon=10^{-20}). A decaying learning rate η⁡(t)=η0​t−0.8\eta(t)=\eta_{0}t^{-0.8} is chosen to comply with Assumptions (LR-MSD) and (LR-Adam) (as t−0.8=o(t−1/2)t^{-0.8}=\mathrm{o}\left(t^{-1/2}\right)). See Appendix D for additional details.

Results are shown in Figure 1. As expected, NGD (with and without momentum) maximizes the ℓ2\ell_{2} margin, while Signum and Adam maximize the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} margin and Muon maximizes ‖⋅‖msp{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{msp}}. These findings seem to hold empirically for ReLU as well as squared ReLU, although the latter tends to achieve a higher margin value for ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-maximizing algorithms. Signum appears to outperform Adam in terms of ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} margin, which is expected considering that the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty}-margin-maximization properties of Adam may hinge on its similarity to sign gradient descent, of which Signum is a closer approximation. Also, we observe that NGD is second-best to Muon when maximizing ‖⋅‖msp{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}_{\mathrm{msp}}, a phenomenon perhaps explained by the fact that the spectral norm of the output layer is its ℓ2\ell_{2} norm. In Appendix D (Figure 2) we compare Muon-Adam with Muon and Adam, and show that it maximizes the appropriate margin.

To test the assumption of directional convergence  (T2), Figure 1(b) shows the cosine similarity of the iterates to the last iterate, ⟨𝜽t‖𝜽t‖2,𝜽last‖𝜽last‖2⟩\left\langle\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}},\frac{\bm{\theta}_{\text{last}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{\text{last}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right\rangle. Note that here the x-axis is a linear time scale normalized with respect to the total training time. We observe, for example, that for all algorithms, alignment is above 0.990.99 for the entire second half of the trajectory, suggesting that directional convergence indeed holds. All trajectories have the margin γ⁡(𝜽t)\gamma(\bm{\theta}_{t}) bounded away from 00 for the entire late phase of training, validating γ⁡(𝜽¯)>0\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0. Also, Assumption (T1) holds in all experiments.

7 Conclusion

In this work we examined the properties of normalized steepest descent in homogeneous models, as well as those of the popular momentum-based optimizers Adam and Muon on smooth homogeneous models. The technical bridge between the two is the unifying perspective of approximate steepest descent, a framework we believe to be general and widely applicable to first-order optimization methods related to the steepest descent family. In the case of momentum-based optimizers we crucially show that the momentum mechanism is asymptotically faithful to the significant gradient coordinates, when the learning rate decays. Our treatment of Muon and Muon-Signum is only a special case of compositions of normalized momentum steepest descent algorithms, while results for Adam and Muon-Adam rely directly on the framework of approximate steepest descent.

Several important questions remain open. First, our results for momentum-based optimizers hold also for non-smooth models under a strong trajectory Assumption (T3), as discussed in Section 4. It is unclear whether these algorithms have a provable margin-maximization bias for non-smooth models, notably ReLU networks, with no such assumptions, or whether Assumption (T3) can be formally proved in certain settings. Second, our results assume directional convergence of the parameters. For gradient descent, the implicit bias in homogeneous models was analyzed by Lyu and Li (2019) before Ji and Telgarsky (2020) formally proved directional convergence; a natural question is whether a directional-convergence guarantee can also be proved for Adam and Muon. Third, the implicit bias of gradient descent was analyzed also for certain non-homogeneous models (Nacson et al., 2019a; Kunin et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2025), and it would be interesting to show such results for other optimizers.

Finally, exploring the theoretical and practical implications of our results is an intriguing research direction. In which settings can generalization of models be deliberately improved with an informed choice of optimizer? Are training-data reconstruction attacks based on satisfaction of KKT conditions, as shown in Haim et al. (2022); Buzaglo et al. (2023); Oz et al. (2024) for gradient descent, also feasible for Adam and Muon? What are the implications of the implicit bias in these optimizers for adversarial robustness (Vardi et al., 2022; Frei et al., 2023)? We hope that our results will help advance understanding of the above questions.

Appendix A Clarke Subgradients and Chain Rule

Our notion of the subgradient of a function f=f⁡(𝜽):ℝp→ℝf=f(\bm{\theta}):\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is that of Clarke (1975):

∂f(𝜽):=conv{limk→∞∇f(𝜽k)∣limk→∞𝜽k=𝜽,f is differentiable at 𝜽k},\partial f(\bm{\theta}):=\mathrm{conv}\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(\bm{\theta}_{k})\mid\lim_{k\to\infty}\bm{\theta}_{k}=\bm{\theta},f\text{ is differentiable at }\bm{\theta}_{k}\right\}, (13)

where conv⁡(⋅)\mathrm{conv}(\cdot) is the convex hull of a set (the set of finite convex combinations of points from that set).

The following basic chain rule holds for all locally Lipschitz functions.

Theorem A.1 (Theorem 2.3.9 and 2.3.10 in Clarke (1990)).

Let f1,…,fm:ℝp→ℝf_{1},\ldots,f_{m}:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}, ℒ:ℝm→ℝ\mathcal{L}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz functions and define 𝐟=(f1,…,fm)\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}). Let (ℒ∘𝐟)​(𝛉)=ℒ⁡(f1​(𝛉),…,fm​(𝛉)):ℝp→ℝ(\mathcal{L}\circ\mathbf{f})(\bm{\theta})=\mathcal{L}(f_{1}(\bm{\theta}),\ldots,f_{m}(\bm{\theta})):\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} be the composition of ℒ\mathcal{L} with ff. Then, it holds:

∂(ℒ∘𝐟)(𝜽)⊆conv{∑i=1mαi𝐡i:𝜶∈∂ℒ(f1(𝜽),…,fm(𝜽)),𝐡i∈∂fi(𝜽)}.\partial(\mathcal{L}\circ\mathbf{f})(\bm{\theta})\subseteq\mathrm{conv}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i}:\bm{\alpha}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{1}(\bm{\theta}),\ldots,f_{m}(\bm{\theta})),\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\partial f_{i}(\bm{\theta})\right\}~. (14)

The following corollary holds for a smooth ℒ\mathcal{L}, and implies in our setting for the loss ℒ⁡(𝜽)=ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐱1,𝜽),…,f⁡(𝐱m,𝜽))\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})=\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}_{1};\bm{\theta}),\dots,f(\mathbf{x}_{m};\bm{\theta})) that any 𝐠∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽)\mathbf{g}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}) is given as a sum 𝐠=∑i=1mℓ′​(yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽))​yi​𝐡i\mathbf{g}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell^{\prime}(y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}))y_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i} where ℓ′\ell^{\prime} is the derivative of the per-sample loss, and 𝐡i∈∂f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽)\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}).

Corollary A.2 (Chain Rule with an Outer Smooth Function).

Let f1,…,fm:ℝp→ℝf_{1},\ldots,f_{m}:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz and ℒ:ℝm→ℝ\mathcal{L}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} be C1C^{1}. Then

∂(ℒ∘𝐟)(𝜽)⊆{∑i=1mαi𝐡i:𝜶∈∂ℒ(f1(𝜽),…,fm(𝜽)),𝐡i∈∂fi(𝜽)}.\partial(\mathcal{L}\circ\mathbf{f})(\bm{\theta})\subseteq\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i}:\bm{\alpha}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{1}(\bm{\theta}),\ldots,f_{m}(\bm{\theta})),\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\partial f_{i}(\bm{\theta})\right\}~. (15)
Proof.

Denote

A={∑i=1mαi𝐡i:𝜶∈∂ℒ(f1(𝜽),…,fm(𝜽)),𝐡i∈∂fi(𝜽)}.A=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i}:\bm{\alpha}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{1}(\bm{\theta}),\ldots,f_{m}(\bm{\theta})),\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\partial f_{i}(\bm{\theta})\right\}~.

Using Theorem A.1, it suffices to show that conv​A⊆A\text{conv}A\subseteq A. Indeed, let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, 𝜶(j)∈∂ℒ⁡(f1​(𝜽),…,fm​(𝜽)),𝐡i(j)∈∂fi​(𝜽)\bm{\alpha}^{(j)}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{1}(\bm{\theta}),\ldots,f_{m}(\bm{\theta})),\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(j)}\in\partial f_{i}(\bm{\theta}) for i∈[m],j∈[n]i\in[m],j\in[n] and let λj>0,j∈[n]\lambda_{j}>0,j\in[n] with ∑j=1nλj=1\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}=1. Since ℒ∈C1\mathcal{L}\in C^{1}, ∂ℒ={∇ℒ}\partial\mathcal{L}=\{\nabla\mathcal{L}\} is unique at any point, so in fact ∀j∈[n]:𝜶(j)=∇ℒ​(f1​(𝜽),…,fm​(𝜽))=:𝜶\forall j\in[n]:\bm{\alpha}^{(j)}=\nabla\mathcal{L}(f_{1}(\bm{\theta}),...,f_{m}(\bm{\theta}))=:\bm{\alpha}, and

∑j=1nλj​∑i=1mαi(j)​𝐡i(j)=∑j=1nλj​∑i=1mαi​𝐡i(j)=∑i=1mαi​∑j=1nλj​𝐡i(j).\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}^{(j)}\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(j)}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(j)}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(j)}~.

Since ∂fi​(𝜽)\partial f_{i}(\bm{\theta}) is convex by definition, ∑j=1nλj​𝐡i(j)∈∂fi​(𝜽)\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(j)}\in\partial f_{i}(\bm{\theta}), so we are finished. ∎

We also consider the notion of Whitney-C1C^{1} stratifiability. We refer the reader to Section 5.2 in Davis et al. (2020) for a technical introduction to the topic. For our purposes, it suffices to know that if f:ℝp→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is Whitney-C1C^{1} stratifiable, its graph is a finite union of C1C^{1} manifolds (implying that (T3) follows from (T2) for some trajectories), with conditions along the boundaries allowing us to assume that ff admits a chain rule.

Definition A.3.

𝜽t:[0,∞)→ℝp\bm{\theta}_{t}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{p} is an arc if it is absolutely continuous on every compact interval, or equivalently if there exists 𝜽t′:[0,∞)→ℝp\bm{\theta}^{\prime}_{t}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{p} which is Lebesgue integrable on every interval [0,t][0,t] so that

∀t≥0:𝜽t=𝜽0+∫0t𝜽s′​𝑑s.\forall t\geq 0:\bm{\theta}_{t}=\bm{\theta}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\bm{\theta}^{\prime}_{s}ds~.

In all the trajectories we discuss, 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} is defined as an integral over d​𝜽td​t\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}, so 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} is an arc.

Theorem A.4 (Chain Rule for Arcs and Stratifiable Functions - Theorem 5.8 in Davis et al. (2020)).

If f:ℝp→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is locally Lipschitz and Whitney C1C^{1}-stratifiable, then for any arc 𝛉t:[0,∞)→ℝp\bm{\theta}_{t}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{p}, almost all t≥0t\geq 0, and all 𝐠∈∂f⁡(𝛉t)\mathbf{g}\in\partial f(\bm{\theta}_{t}), it holds:

d​f​(𝜽t)d​t=⟨𝐠,d​𝜽td​t⟩.\frac{df(\bm{\theta}_{t})}{dt}=\left\langle\mathbf{g},\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rangle~. (16)

Finally, we also need a chain rule for the norm ‖𝜽t‖\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert. We may circumvent the requirement that ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert be C1C^{1}-stratifiable with the following definition and theorem:

Definition A.5 (Subdifferentially Regular Functions - Definition 5.3 in Davis et al. (2020)).

f:ℝp→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is said to be subdifferentially regular if ∀𝜽∈ℝp,𝐠∈∂f⁡(𝜽)\forall\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},\mathbf{g}\in\partial f(\bm{\theta}),

f⁡(𝜽′)≥f⁡(𝜽)+⟨𝐠,𝜽′−𝜽⟩+o⁡(‖𝜽′−𝜽‖)as 𝜽′→𝜽.f(\bm{\theta}^{\prime})\geq f(\bm{\theta})+\left\langle\mathbf{g},\bm{\theta}^{\prime}-\bm{\theta}\right\rangle+\mathrm{o}\left(\left\lVert\bm{\theta}^{\prime}-\bm{\theta}\right\rVert\right)\quad\text{as $\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\to\bm{\theta}$}~.

In particular, any convex function, including any norm, satisfies the above inequality without an error term o⁡(‖𝜽′−𝜽‖)\mathrm{o}\left(\left\lVert\bm{\theta}^{\prime}-\bm{\theta}\right\rVert\right) and thus is subdifferentially regular.

Theorem A.6 (Chain Rule for Arcs and Subdifferentially Regular Functions - Lemma 5.4 in Davis et al. (2020)).

If f:ℝp→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is locally Lipschitz and subdifferentially regular, then for any arc 𝛉t:[0,∞)→ℝp\bm{\theta}_{t}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{p}, almost all t≥0t\geq 0, and all 𝐠∈∂f⁡(𝛉t)\mathbf{g}\in\partial f(\bm{\theta}_{t}), it holds:

d​f​(𝜽t)d​t=⟨𝐠,d​𝜽td​t⟩.\frac{df(\bm{\theta}_{t})}{dt}=\left\langle\mathbf{g},\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rangle~. (17)

For reference, the following is a standard characterization of the subdifferential of a norm:

∂‖𝜽‖={𝐯∈ℝp∣⟨𝐯,𝜽⟩=‖𝜽‖,‖𝐯‖⋆≤1}.\partial\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert=\left\{\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\mid\left\langle\mathbf{v},\bm{\theta}\right\rangle=\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert,{\left\lVert\mathbf{v}\right\rVert}_{\star}\leq 1\right\}~. (18)

Note that by definition of the dual norm it holds that ⟨𝐯,𝜽⟩≤‖𝜽‖​‖𝐯‖⋆\left\langle\mathbf{v},\bm{\theta}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert{\left\lVert\mathbf{v}\right\rVert}_{\star}, so in fact when 𝜽≠𝟎\bm{\theta}\neq{\mathbf{0}}, ‖𝐯‖⋆=1{\left\lVert\mathbf{v}\right\rVert}_{\star}=1 for any 𝐯∈∂‖𝜽‖\mathbf{v}\in\partial\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert.

Appendix B Momentum (EMA)

B.1 Discrete Momentum

For a parameter β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) and a real-valued sequence gn,n≥1g_{n},n\geq 1, discrete momentum mnm_{n} is defined as follows:

mn=β​mn−1+(1−β)​gn,m0=0,m_{n}=\beta m_{n-1}+(1-\beta)g_{n},\quad m_{0}=0~, (19)

with the explicit solution:

mn=(1−β)​∑k=1nβn−k​gk.m_{n}=(1-\beta)\sum_{k=1}^{n}\beta^{n-k}g_{k}~.

We give for reference the definition of Adam in the discrete case for a sequence of subgradients 𝐠n\mathbf{g}_{n}, parameters β1,β2∈(0,1)\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in(0,1), a learning rate ηn\eta_{n} and a constant ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 (in our analysis ε=0\varepsilon=0). Square, division and square root are taken elementwise.

Adam (Discrete):

𝐦n\displaystyle\mathbf{m}_{n} =β1​𝐦n−1+(1−β1)​𝐠n,𝐦0=𝟎\displaystyle=\beta_{1}\mathbf{m}_{n-1}+(1-\beta_{1})\mathbf{g}_{n},\quad\mathbf{m}_{0}={\mathbf{0}} (20)
𝐯n\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{n} =β2​𝐯n−1+(1−β2)​𝐠n2,𝐯0=𝟎\displaystyle=\beta_{2}\mathbf{v}_{n-1}+(1-\beta_{2})\mathbf{g}_{n}^{2},\quad\mathbf{v}_{0}={\mathbf{0}}
𝐦^n\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{n} =(1−β1n)−1​𝐦n,𝐯^n=(1−β2n)−1​𝐯n\displaystyle=(1-\beta_{1}^{n})^{-1}\mathbf{m}_{n},\quad\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{n}=(1-\beta_{2}^{n})^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{n}
Δ​𝜽n\displaystyle\Delta\bm{\theta}_{n} =−ηn​𝐦^n𝐯^n+ε.\displaystyle=-\eta_{n}\frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{n}}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{n}}+\varepsilon}~.

B.2 Continuous Momentum

Notice that Equation (19) shows that the direction of update of mnm_{n} is gn−mn−1g_{n}-m_{n-1}:

mn−mn−1=(1−β)​(gn−mn−1).m_{n}-m_{n-1}=(1-\beta)(g_{n}-m_{n-1})~.

The natural analogue for a continuous time variable tt and a parameter c>0c>0 is therefore:

d​mtd​t=c⁡(gt−mt),m0=0.\frac{dm_{t}}{dt}=c(g_{t}-m_{t}),\quad m_{0}=0~.

This equation has the following explicit solution, clearly of a similar form to the discrete version:

mt=∫0tc​e−c⁡(t−s)​gs​𝑑s.m_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}ce^{-c(t-s)}g_{s}ds~.

This form is identical to (Wang et al., 2021), with the caveat that they assumed c=1−βc=1-\beta, a form restricting cc to small values (note that taking c→∞c\to\infty induces the regime mt=gtm_{t}=g_{t}). To clearly uncover the connection between β\beta and cc, assume that a discrete momentum iteration takes a unit time Δ​t=1\Delta t=1, and that steps are small enough so that gsg_{s} is roughly constant on [t,t+1][t,t+1]. Then

mt+1−mt\displaystyle m_{t+1}-m_{t} =∫0t+1c​e−c⁡(t+1−s)​gs​𝑑s−∫0tc​e−c⁡(t−s)​gs​𝑑s=(e−c−1)​mt+∫tt+1c​e−c⁡(t+1−s)​gs​𝑑s\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t+1}ce^{-c(t+1-s)}g_{s}ds-\int_{0}^{t}ce^{-c(t-s)}g_{s}ds=(e^{-c}-1)m_{t}+\int_{t}^{t+1}ce^{-c(t+1-s)}g_{s}ds
≈(e−c−1)​mt+(1−e−c)​gt=(1−e−c)​(gt−mt).\displaystyle\approx(e^{-c}-1)m_{t}+(1-e^{-c})g_{t}=(1-e^{-c})(g_{t}-m_{t})~.

So cc is analogous to −log⁡β-\log\beta, hence spanning the entire range (0,∞)(0,\infty). When β\beta is close to 11 we obtain c≈(1−β)c\approx(1-\beta).

In the definition of discrete Adam, a multiplicative factor of (1−βn)−1(1-\beta^{n})^{-1} is used to correct the initial bias accrued when initializing m0=0m_{0}=0. The continuous analogue for the bias correction is (1−e−c​t)−1(1-e^{-ct})^{-1}, since for small tt, mt≈g0​∫0tc​e−c⁡(t−s)​𝑑s=g0​(1−e−c​t)m_{t}\approx g_{0}\int_{0}^{t}ce^{-c(t-s)}ds=g_{0}(1-e^{-ct}).

Definition B.1.

We denote

ℱ=Lloc∞([0,∞)),𝒢={g:[0,∞)→ℝ∣∃τ>0,ρ>0:g2(t)>ρ a.e. on [0,τ]},\mathcal{F}=L^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}([0,\infty)),\quad\mathcal{G}=\left\{g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\mid\exists\tau>0,\rho>0:g^{2}(t)>\rho\text{ a.e. on }[0,\tau]\right\}~,

where Lloc∞​([0,∞))L^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}([0,\infty)) is the space of Lebesgue measurable functions g⁡(t):[0,∞)→ℝg(t):[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} so that g⁡(t)g(t) is essentially bounded (bounded except on a measure zero set) on every compact interval [a,b][a,b]. We denote also for convenience

M[a,b]​(g):=ess​sup[a,b]|g|.M_{[a,b]}(g):=\text{ess}\sup_{[a,b]}\left|g\right|~.

It is a standard fact that Lloc∞​([0,∞))⊆Llocp​([0,∞))L^{\infty}_{\text{loc}}([0,\infty))\subseteq L^{p}_{\text{loc}}([0,\infty)) for any p≥1p\geq 1, the latter being the space of functions gg with ∫[a,b]|g|p<∞\int_{[a,b]}|g|^{p}<\infty on every compact interval [a,b][a,b]. This allows us to define the momentum expression for gg. The class 𝒢\mathcal{G} encapsulates Assumption (A1), facilitating a discussion of the Adam ratio.

Definition B.2 (Momentum/EMA).

Let g⁡(t)∈ℱg(t)\in\mathcal{F}. For a parameter c>0c>0 denote the following by EMA​(g,c)​(t)\mathrm{EMA}\left(g,c\right)(t) or A​(g,c)​(t)A(g,c)(t) for short:

EMA⁡(g,c)​(t)=A⁡(g,c)​(t):=∫0tc​e−c⁡(t−s)​g​(s)​𝑑s.\mathrm{EMA}\left(g,c\right)(t)=A(g,c)(t):=\int_{0}^{t}ce^{-c(t-s)}g(s)ds~.

Also denote for convenience:

I⁡(g,c)​(t)=∫0tec​s​g​(s)​𝑑s,I∞​(g,c)=limt→∞I⁡(g,c)​(t),I(g,c)(t)=\int_{0}^{t}e^{cs}g(s)ds,\quad I_{\infty}(g,c)=\lim_{t\to\infty}I(g,c)(t)~,

so A⁡(g,c)​(t)=c​e−c​t​I​(g,c)​(t)A(g,c)(t)=ce^{-ct}I(g,c)(t).

We prove a series of useful lemmas about the properties of the EMA.

Lemma B.3 (Momentum ODE).

Let g⁡(t)∈ℱg(t)\in\mathcal{F} and c>0c>0. Then for almost any t≥0t\geq 0,

d​A​(g,c)d​t=c⁡(g⁡(t)−A⁡(g,c)​(t)).\frac{dA(g,c)}{dt}=c\left(g(t)-A(g,c)(t)\right)~.
Proof.

Since gg is Lebesgue integrable, by differentiation rules and the fundamental theorem of calculus we have

d​A​(g,c)d​t=−c2​e−c​t​I​(g,c)​(t)+c​e−c​t​d​I​(g,c)d​t=−c​A​(g,c)​(t)+c​e−c​t​ec​t​g​(t)=c⁡(g⁡(t)−A⁡(g,c)​(t))\frac{dA(g,c)}{dt}=-c^{2}e^{-ct}I(g,c)(t)+ce^{-ct}\frac{dI(g,c)}{dt}=-cA(g,c)(t)+ce^{-ct}e^{ct}g(t)=c(g(t)-A(g,c)(t))

∎

Lemma B.4 (Uniform Bound on Adam Ratio).

Let g⁡(t)∈ℱg(t)\in\mathcal{F} and c1>c22>0c_{1}>\frac{c_{2}}{2}>0. Then,

|A⁡(g,c1)​(t)|≤A⁡(|g|,c1)​(t)≤c1c2​(2​c1−c2)​A⁡(g2,c2)​(t).\left|A(g,c_{1})(t)\right|\leq A(\left|g\right|,c_{1})(t)\leq\frac{c_{1}}{\sqrt{c_{2}(2c_{1}-c_{2})}}\sqrt{A(g^{2},c_{2})(t)}~.

A⁡(|g|,c1)​(t)≤𝒪⁡(A⁡(g2,c2)​(t)),A(\left|g\right|,c_{1})(t)\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{A(g^{2},c_{2})(t)}\right)~,

≤c1​(∫0te−c2​(t−s)​g2​(s)​𝑑s)12​(∫0te−(2​c1−c2)​(t−s)​𝑑s)12\displaystyle\leq c_{1}\left(\int_{0}^{t}e^{-c_{2}(t-s)}g^{2}(s)ds\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{0}^{t}e^{-(2c_{1}-c_{2})(t-s)}ds\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}
≤c1c2​A⁡(g2,c2)​(t)​(1−e−(2​c1−c2)​t2​c1−c2)12\displaystyle\leq\frac{c_{1}}{\sqrt{c_{2}}}\sqrt{A\left(g^{2},c_{2}\right)(t)}\left(\frac{1-e^{-(2c_{1}-c_{2})t}}{2c_{1}-c_{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}

Appendix C Proof Details

C.1 Losses

In this work we consider log-concave, exponentially-tailed losses. Namely, we consider a loss of the form

ℒ⁡(𝜽)=∑i=1mℓ⁡(yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)),\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\ell(y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}))~,

where ℓ⁡(u)=e−φ⁡(u)\ell(u)=e^{-\varphi(u)}, and φ∈C2​(ℝ)\varphi\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}) with ∃ΦM′,ΦM′′>0:∀u∈ℝ:0<φ′​(u)≤ΦM′,0≤φ′′​(u)≤ΦM′′\exists\Phi_{M}^{\prime},\Phi_{M}^{\prime\prime}>0:\forall u\in\mathbb{R}:0<\varphi^{\prime}(u)\leq\Phi_{M}^{\prime},0\leq\varphi^{\prime\prime}(u)\leq\Phi_{M}^{\prime\prime}.

Note that ℓ∈(ℓexp,ℓlog)\ell\in(\ell_{\mathrm{exp}},\ell_{\mathrm{log}}) satisfy this:

ℓexp​(u)=e−u=e−φexp​(u),ℓlog​(u)=log⁡(1+e−u)=e−φlog​(u),\ell_{\mathrm{exp}}(u)=e^{-u}=e^{-\varphi_{\exp}(u)},\quad\ell_{\mathrm{log}}(u)=\log(1+e^{-u})=e^{-\varphi_{\log}(u)}~,

for

φexp​(u)=u,φlog​(u)=−log⁡log⁡(1+e−u).\varphi_{\exp}(u)=u,\quad\varphi_{\log}(u)=-\log\log(1+e^{-u})~.

The conditions on φ\varphi imply the following:

  1. 1.

    φ\varphi is strictly monotone increasing and ℓ\ell is strictly monotone decreasing. Also u↦φ′​(u)​uu\mapsto\varphi^{\prime}(u)u is strictly monotone increasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty):

    d​φ′​(u)​ud​u=φ′′​(u)​u+φ′​(u)≥φ′​(u)>0.\frac{d\varphi^{\prime}(u)u}{du}=\varphi^{\prime\prime}(u)u+\varphi^{\prime}(u)\geq\varphi^{\prime}(u)>0~.
  2. 2.

    For any u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, φ\varphi has at least a linear growth rate on [u0,∞)[u_{0},\infty):

    φ⁡(u)−φ⁡(u0)=∫u0uφ′​(w)​𝑑w≥φ′​(u0)​(u−u0).\varphi(u)-\varphi(u_{0})=\int_{u_{0}}^{u}\varphi^{\prime}(w)dw\geq\varphi^{\prime}(u_{0})(u-u_{0})~. (23)

    In particular φ⁡(u)​⟶u→∞​∞\varphi(u)\overset{u\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty.

  3. 3.

    φ\varphi has a strictly monotone increasing inverse φ−1\varphi^{-1} defined on φ⁡(ℝ)\varphi(\mathbb{R}). In particular φ−1\varphi^{-1} is defined on [φ⁡(0),∞)[\varphi(0),\infty), φ−1​(u)​⟶u→∞​∞\varphi^{-1}(u)\overset{u\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty, and (φ−1)′(\varphi^{-1})^{\prime} is nonincreasing since (φ−1)′​(u)=1φ′​(φ−1​(u))\left(\varphi^{-1}\right)^{\prime}(u)=\frac{1}{\varphi^{\prime}(\varphi^{-1}(u))} and φ−1,φ′\varphi^{-1},\varphi^{\prime} are increasing. This implies also that (φ−1)′(\varphi^{-1})^{\prime} is bounded on [φ⁡(0),∞)[\varphi(0),\infty).

  4. 4.

    For any a∈ℝ∪{±∞}a\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}, limu→aℓ⁡(u)=0\lim_{u\to a}\ell(u)=0 implies limu→aφ⁡(u)=∞\lim_{u\to a}\varphi(u)=\infty, implying a=∞a=\infty, since φ\varphi is bounded on any compact interval and monotone increasing. Note that since the same is true of φ−1\varphi^{-1}, this implies also that if limu→aφ−1​(u)=∞\lim_{u\to a}\varphi^{-1}(u)=\infty then a=∞a=\infty.

C.2 Algorithm-Independent KKT Stationarity

In this section we provide general insight into properties of trajectories of homogeneous models, culminating in Theorem C.8 which shows that KKT stationarity of a limit point of 𝜽t‖𝜽t‖\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert} with respect to Problem (11) follows from decay of the loss and alignment between gradients and parameters.

Definition C.1 (Hard and Soft Margins).

Let f⁡(𝐱,𝜽)f(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}) be a model satisfying (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak). We denote the “hard” and “soft” margins γ​(𝜽),γ~​(𝜽)\gamma(\bm{\theta}),\widetilde{\gamma}(\bm{\theta}) for 𝜽≠0\bm{\theta}\neq 0 as follows:

γ⁡(𝜽):=mini∈[m]⁡yi​f​(xi,𝜽‖𝜽‖),γ~​(𝜽):=φ−1​(log⁡1ℒ⁡(𝜽))‖𝜽‖L.\gamma(\bm{\theta}):=\min_{i\in[m]}y_{i}f\left(x_{i};\frac{\bm{\theta}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert}\right),\quad\widetilde{\gamma}(\bm{\theta}):=\frac{\varphi^{-1}\left(\log\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})}\right)}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert^{L}}~.

Note that γ~\widetilde{\gamma} is well defined whenever log⁡1ℒ⁡(𝜽)∈φ⁡(ℝ)\log\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})}\in\varphi(\mathbb{R}), and in particular whenever log⁡1ℒ⁡(𝜽)>φ⁡(0)\log\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})}>\varphi(0).

In this work we prove KKT stationarity using the notion of approximate KKT points.

Definition C.3.

We say 𝜽\bm{\theta} is a feasible point of Problem (11) if ∀i∈[m]:yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)≥1\forall i\in[m]:y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})\geq 1, or equivalently if qmin​(𝜽)≥1q_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{\theta})\geq 1.

Definition C.4.

A feasible point 𝜽\bm{\theta} of Problem (11) is called an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-approximate KKT point if there exist λ1,…,λm≥0\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{m}\geq 0, 𝐡i∈∂f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽)\mathbf{h}_{i}\in\partial f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta}) and 𝐤∈∂12​‖𝜽‖2\mathbf{k}\in\partial\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert^{2} with

  1. 1.

    ‖∑i=1mλi​yi​𝐡i−𝐤‖2≤ε\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}y_{i}\mathbf{h}_{i}-\mathbf{k}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon.

  2. 2.

    ∑i=1mλi​(yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)−1)≤δ\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{i}(y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})-1)\leq\delta.

Definition C.5.

We say that a feasible point of Problem (11) satisfies the Mangasarian-Fromovitz Constraint Qualifications if there exists 𝐯∈ℝp\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} such that for all i∈[m]i\in[m] with 1−yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)=01-y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})=0 and for all 𝐡∈∂(1−yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽))\mathbf{h}\in\partial\left(1-y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})\right), it holds:

⟨𝐯,𝐡⟩>0.\left\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}\right\rangle>0. (30)
Lemma C.6 (Lemma A.11 in Tsilivis et al. (2025)).

The MFCQ constraints are satisfied by any feasible point 𝛉\bm{\theta} of Problem (11) for ff satisfying, (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak).

Theorem C.7 (Theorem C.4 in Lyu and Li (2019) + Lemma C.6).

Let 𝛉n→𝛉\bm{\theta}_{n}\rightarrow\bm{\theta} be a converging sequence so that 𝛉n\bm{\theta}_{n} is a (εn,δn)(\varepsilon_{n},\delta_{n})-approximate KKT point of Problem (11), where εn→0,δn→0\varepsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0,\delta_{n}\rightarrow 0. Then 𝛉\bm{\theta} is a KKT point of Problem (11).

Theorem C.8 (KKT Stationarity Derived from Alignment).

Let 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} be any arc of parameters of a model f⁡(𝐱,𝛉)f(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}) assuming (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak), and denote 𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝛉t)\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) any choice of subgradient along the trajectory. Let 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} with ‖𝛉¯‖=1,γ⁡(𝛉¯)>0\left\lVert\bar{\bm{\theta}}\right\rVert=1,\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0. Assume that there exists a sequence tnt_{n} with 𝛉tn≠𝟎,𝐠tn≠𝟎\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\neq{\mathbf{0}},\mathbf{g}_{t_{n}}\neq{\mathbf{0}} and:

  1. 1.

    ℒ⁡(𝜽tn)​⟶n→∞​0\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}})\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0

  2. 2.

    𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖​⟶n→∞​𝜽¯\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\bar{\bm{\theta}}

  3. 3.

    ⟨𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖,−𝐠tn‖𝐠tn‖⋆⟩​⟶n→∞​1\left\langle\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t_{n}}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}1.

Then 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} is the direction of a KKT point of Equation (11).

Proof.

First, note that since ℒ⁡(𝜽tn)​⟶n→∞​0\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}})\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0, it holds that ‖𝜽tn‖​⟶n→∞​∞,qmintn​⟶n→∞​∞\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty,q_{\mathrm{min}}^{t_{n}}\overset{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty. Since γ⁡(𝜽tn)\gamma(\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}) converges to γ⁡(𝜽¯)>0\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0, in particular for large enough nn, γ⁡(𝜽tn)>12​γ​(𝜽¯)>0\gamma(\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}})>\frac{1}{2}\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0. Therefore it holds by Lemma C.2 that for large enough nn, there exists C>0C>0 with

‖𝐠tn‖⋆≥C​ℒ​(𝜽tn)​‖𝜽tn‖L−1.{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}_{\star}\geq C\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}})\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert^{L-1}~.

Now, any 𝜽\bm{\theta} with γ⁡(𝜽)>0\gamma(\bm{\theta})>0 has for all i∈[m]i\in[m] that yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽)>0y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})>0 and therefore there exists a feasible point 𝜽~\widetilde{\bm{\theta}} of Equation (11) along its direction with qmin​(𝜽~)=1q_{\mathrm{min}}(\widetilde{\bm{\theta}})=1, given by

𝜽~:=𝜽qmin​(𝜽)1/L=𝜽mini∈[m]⁡(yi​f​(𝐱i,𝜽))1/L=𝜽γ​(𝜽)1/L​‖𝜽‖.\widetilde{\bm{\theta}}:=\frac{\bm{\theta}}{q_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{\theta})^{1/L}}=\frac{\bm{\theta}}{\min_{i\in[m]}\left(y_{i}f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\bm{\theta})\right)^{1/L}}=\frac{\bm{\theta}}{\gamma(\bm{\theta})^{1/L}\left\lVert\bm{\theta}\right\rVert}~.

Denote 𝜽^:=𝜽¯~=𝜽¯γ​(𝜽¯)1/L\hat{\bm{\theta}}:=\widetilde{\bar{\bm{\theta}}}=\frac{\bar{\bm{\theta}}}{\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})^{1/L}}. We claim 𝜽^\hat{\bm{\theta}} is the desired KKT point. We show that in fact 𝜽^\hat{\bm{\theta}} is itself a (εs,δs)(\varepsilon_{s},\delta_{s})-approximate KKT point for arbitrarily small (εs,δs)(\varepsilon_{s},\delta_{s}), allowing us to use Theorem C.7 with the constant sequence 𝜽^\hat{\bm{\theta}}.

First note that by continuity and scale-invariance of γ⁡(𝜽)\gamma(\bm{\theta}), it holds that

Theorem C.11 (KKT Stationarity for NSD - Theorem 3.2).

Let 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} be a trajectory of normalized steepest descent with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert (Equation (3)) under Assumptions (M1-Weak), (M2-Weak), (R1), (LR-NSD). ‖𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖−𝜽¯‖\displaystyle\left\lVert\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}\right\rVert ≤‖𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖−𝜽sn‖𝜽sn‖‖+‖𝜽sn‖𝜽sn‖−𝜽¯‖≤‖𝜽tn‖𝜽tn‖−𝜽sn‖𝜽sn‖‖+1n\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}-\frac{\bm{\theta}_{s_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{s_{n}}\right\rVert}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\frac{\bm{\theta}_{s_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{s_{n}}\right\rVert}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t_{n}}\right\rVert}-\frac{\bm{\theta}_{s_{n}}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{s_{n}}\right\rVert}\right\rVert+\frac{1}{n}
≤1n+∫sntn‖d​𝜽t‖𝜽t‖d​t‖​𝑑t≤1n+2​∫sntn‖d​𝜽td​t‖‖𝜽t‖​𝑑t≤3n→0,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}+\int_{s_{n}}^{t_{n}}\left\lVert\frac{d\frac{\bm{\theta}_{t}}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}}{dt}\right\rVert dt\leq\frac{1}{n}+2\int_{s_{n}}^{t_{n}}\frac{\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert}{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}dt\leq\frac{3}{n}\rightarrow 0~,

C.4 Approximate Steepest Descent

In this section we prove a KKT result for trajectories 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} approximating steepest descent. We provide the following definition:

Definition C.12 (Approximate Steepest Descent).

We say an arc 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} is a trajectory of Approximate Steepest Descent with respect to a norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert if eventually ∃𝐠t≠𝟎∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)\exists\mathbf{g}_{t}\neq{\mathbf{0}}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) for almost any tt, and there exist ν⁡(t)>0,Rmax>0\nu(t)>0,R_{\text{max}}>0 with:

  1. 1.

    limt→∞N⁡(t):=limt→∞∫0tν=∞\lim_{t\to\infty}N(t):=\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{0}^{t}\nu=\infty

  2. 2.

    lim supt→∞‖𝜽t‖N⁡(t)≤Rmax\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}{N(t)}\leq R_{\text{max}}

  3. 3.

    ess​liminft→∞⁡r​(t)≥1\essliminf_{t\to\infty}r(t)\geq 1, where

    r⁡(t)​=a.e.​sup𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)∖{𝟎}⟨1ν⁡(t)​d​𝜽td​t,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩.r(t)\overset{a.e.}{=}\sup_{\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\setminus\{{\mathbf{0}}\}}\left\langle\frac{1}{\nu(t)}\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle~.

Note that as ∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) is a compact set for any locally Lipschitz ℒ\mathcal{L}, the supremum in the definition of r⁡(t)r(t) is attained by some 𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝜽t)\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}).

Some motivation is in order. A possible and natural choice of ν⁡(t)\nu(t) is ν⁡(t)=‖d​𝜽td​t‖\nu(t)=\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert. This choice is motivated by the fact that for exact Steepest Flow, we have by definition for almost any tt

r⁡(t)=⟨1ν⁡(t)​d​𝜽td​t,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩=1,r(t)=\left\langle\frac{1}{\nu(t)}\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle=1~,

and

‖𝜽t‖≤‖𝜽0‖+∫0tν.\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{0}\right\rVert+\int_{0}^{t}\nu~.

Also, the following type of trajectory, which is a simpler and more “natural” definition of Approximate Steepest Descent, is also covered by our definition when choosing ν⁡(t)=‖d​𝜽td​t‖\nu(t)=\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert:

⟨d​𝜽td​t‖d​𝜽td​t‖,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩​⟶t→∞​1.\left\langle\frac{\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}}{\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}1~.

It is crucial in our analysis for an inner product of this type to tend to 1. However, we can allow ν⁡(t)\nu(t) to be momentarily larger than ‖d​𝜽td​t‖\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert, as long as on average it is not so (condition 2, when Rmax≤1R_{\text{max}}\leq 1). Thus the definition allows more flexibility for adaptive algorithms such as Adam, since we can choose ν⁡(t)\nu(t) as an external learning rate, with d​𝜽td​t\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt} affected both by ν⁡(t)\nu(t) and by the dynamics. In particular this flexibility will be invaluable for the main result of KKT convergence for Adam.

Lemma C.13.

If 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} is an arc with eventually ∃𝐠t≠𝟎∈∂ℒ⁡(𝛉t)\exists\mathbf{g}_{t}\neq{\mathbf{0}}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) for almost any tt, ess​liminf⁡r​(t)≥1\essliminf r(t)\geq 1 for r⁡(t)​=a.e.​sup𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝛉t)∖{𝟎}⟨1ν⁡(t)​d​𝛉td​t,−𝐠t‖𝐠t‖⋆⟩,ν⁡(t)=‖d​𝛉td​t‖r(t)\overset{a.e.}{=}\sup_{\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t})\setminus\{{\mathbf{0}}\}}\left\langle\frac{1}{\nu(t)}\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt},-\frac{\mathbf{g}_{t}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\right\rangle,\nu(t)=\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert, and ∫0tν​⟶t→∞​∞\int_{0}^{t}\nu\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty, then 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} is a trajectory of Approximate Steepest Descent with Rmax≤1R_{\text{max}}\leq 1.

Proof.

According to Definition C.12, it remains to show that lim supt→∞‖𝜽t‖N⁡(t)≤1\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}{N(t)}\leq 1 where N⁡(t)=∫0tν=∫0t‖d​𝜽sd​s‖​𝑑sN(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\nu=\int_{0}^{t}\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{s}}{ds}\right\rVert ds. By the triangle inequalities, ‖𝜽t‖≤‖𝜽0‖+N⁡(t)\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{0}\right\rVert+N(t), and since N⁡(t)​⟶t→∞​∞N(t)\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}\infty,

lim supt→∞‖𝜽t‖N⁡(t)≤lim supt→∞(1+‖𝜽0‖N⁡(t))=1\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\rVert}{N(t)}\leq\limsup_{t\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{\left\lVert\bm{\theta}_{0}\right\rVert}{N(t)}\right)=1

∎

Lemma C.14.

If 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} is a trajectory of Approximate Steepest Descent, then for almost all t≥0t\geq 0 there exists 𝐠t∈∂ℒ⁡(𝛉t)\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) with:

r⁡(t)​ν​(t)=−d​ℒd​t‖𝐠t‖⋆≤‖d​𝜽td​t‖,r(t)\nu(t)=\frac{\frac{-d\mathcal{L}}{dt}}{{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}}\leq\left\lVert\frac{d\bm{\theta}_{t}}{dt}\right\rVert~,

and in particular, d​ℒd​t<0\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dt}<0 for almost all large enough tt.

Proof.

Theorem C.17 (KKT Stationarity for Approximate SD ).

Assume 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} is a trajectory of Approximate Steepest Descent with Rmax≤1R_{\text{max}}\leq 1, and assume that eventually 𝛉t≠𝟎\bm{\theta}_{t}\neq{\mathbf{0}} and 𝛉t\bm{\theta}_{t} converges in direction to some 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} with γ⁡(𝛉¯)>0\gamma(\bar{\bm{\theta}})>0. Then 𝛉¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} is along the direction of a KKT point of Equation (11).

Proof.

Follows from Theorem C.8 using Lemma C.16 and Lemma C.15. ∎

Recall that (T3) is implied if strengthening (M1-Weak) to (M1).

Whenever i∈[m],i¯∉Iji\in[m],\bar{i}\notin I_{j} we have 𝐠t​[i,j]​𝐠t​[i¯,j]=o⁡(‖𝐠t‖⋆2)\mathbf{g}_{t}[i,j]\mathbf{g}_{t}[\bar{i},j]=\mathrm{o}\left({\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}\right) and 𝐯t​[i,i¯,j]=o⁡(‖𝐠t‖⋆2)\mathbf{v}_{t}[i,\bar{i},j]=\mathrm{o}\left({\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}\right) by applying Lemma B.5 2(c) (with g=G2,F=𝐠t​[i,j]​𝐠t​[i¯,j]g=G^{2},F=\mathbf{g}_{t}[i,j]\mathbf{g}_{t}[\bar{i},j]), so

and by Equation (43)

∀i,i′∈Ij:|𝐯t​[i,i′,j]−𝐠t​[i,j]​𝐠t​[i′,j]|=o⁡(𝐠t​[i,j]​𝐠t​[i′,j])=o⁡(‖𝐠t‖⋆2),\forall i,i^{\prime}\in I_{j}:\left|\mathbf{v}_{t}[i,i^{\prime},j]-\mathbf{g}_{t}[i,j]\mathbf{g}_{t}[i^{\prime},j]\right|=\mathrm{o}\left(\mathbf{g}_{t}[i,j]\mathbf{g}_{t}[i^{\prime},j]\right)=\mathrm{o}\left({\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}\right)~,

so

∀j∈[p]:|𝐯t​[j]−𝐠t2​[j]|≤o⁡(‖𝐠t‖⋆2).\forall j\in[p]:\left|\mathbf{v}_{t}[j]-\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}[j]\right|\leq\mathrm{o}\left({\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}\right)~. (45)

Hence,

∀j∈Jε​(t):|𝐯t​[j]𝐠t2​[j]−1|=|𝐯t​[j]−𝐠t2​[j]||𝐠t2​[j]|≤o⁡(‖𝐠t‖⋆2)ε2​‖𝐠t‖⋆2​⟶t→∞​0\forall j\in J_{\varepsilon}(t):\left|\frac{\mathbf{v}_{t}[j]}{\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}[j]}-1\right|=\frac{\left|\mathbf{v}_{t}[j]-\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}[j]\right|}{\left|\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}[j]\right|}\leq\frac{\mathrm{o}\left({\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}\right)}{\varepsilon^{2}{\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}}\overset{t\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0

Notice that from norm equivalence, ‖𝐠t‖⋆2≤𝒪⁡(‖𝐠t‖∞2)=𝒪⁡(‖𝐠t2‖∞)≤𝒪⁡(‖𝐠t2‖⋆){\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert}_{\star}^{2}\leq\mathcal{O}\left(\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}\right\rVert_{\infty}\right)\leq\mathcal{O}\left({\left\lVert\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}\right\rVert}_{\star}\right).
